implementation_notes: Rust enforces both halves of the pattern in the language: struct fields are private to their module by default, so code outside the module cannot read or write them (there are no subclasses to bypass that), and a method taking `&self` cannot mutate the receiver at all - the borrow checker rejects any write unless the field is wrapped in `Cell`, `RefCell` or a lock, which is an explicit, greppable opt-in. Accessors (`fn radius(&self) -> f64`) are therefore written only when the type must hide its representation or uphold an invariant, not as a general convention, because a getter borrows the whole struct and blocks splitting borrows. Use `pub(crate)` or a private module for controlled internal access and `#[non_exhaustive]` for public structs that must stay constructible only through their constructor.
pitfalls: `Cell`/`RefCell`/`Mutex` fields restore interior mutability, so a `&self` method can write them again - keep them out of holders that are supposed to be frozen.
The privacy boundary is the module, not the type: any code in the same module (including child modules) may write the fields, so define the holder in a module of its own when the invariant matters.
Making a field `pub` is a permanent API and semver commitment and getters borrow all of `self`, so accessors are worth writing only where they buy encapsulation or invariant protection.
